results.title: Deconstructed biography is real history
results.description: A friend recently shared with me that his son, a highly accomplished doctor who had spent nearly two decades building a successful career in Saudi Arabia, had decided to return to Kashmir for good. From every practical standpoint, the decision seemed puzzling. He enjoyed professional recognition, financial security, and a comfortable life. My first thought was that the lack of a path to Saudi citizenship had finally compelled him to leave. But I was mistaken. The real reason lay much deeper. His two daughters had reached marriageable age, and the family wanted them to grow up, marry, and build their lives within their own cultural world. Their concern was not religious. Saudi Arabia offered every opportunity to practise Islam. What troubled them was the slow, almost invisible, power of culture. They feared that growing up in a different social environment would gradually shape their daughters’ habits, values, aspirations, and sense of belonging in ways that would distance them from their own society. The story captures a truth that sociology has long recognized: culture often leaves a deeper and more lasting imprint on human life than religion alone. Pierre Bourdieu’s concept of habitus explains how everyday practices, language, tastes, and social relationships become embodied dispositions that quietly reproduce a community across generations. Clifford Geertz described culture as the “webs of significance” through which people understand their world, while Robert Redfield showed that the moral life of communities rests as much on shared customs and local traditions as on formal religious beliefs. This distinction becomes even more significant when we try to understand the choices that shape nations. History rarely allows us to hear the private conversations, moral struggles, or quiet reflections behind great political decisions. More often, it reaches us through official records, later interpretations, and the dominant ideas of an age. The past, therefore, is seldom encountered in its fullness. It is filtered through the language of power, ideology, and memory. Kashmir has long been confined within such inherited narratives. The lives of its principal actors, their intellectual exchanges, and their shared civilizational inheritance have too often been interpreted through the narrow lenses of religion, nationalism, or political conflict. In the process, the deeper cultural and human currents that connected them have receded from view. Few examples illustrate this better than the remarkable trio of Allama Muhammad Iqbal, Jawaharlal Nehru, and Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah. Each occupies an enduring place in Kashmir’s collective memory, yet each is usually remembered through the ideological battles of the twentieth century or through the judgments of admirers and critics. Such readings flatten complex personalities into political symbols. They tell us where these men stood, but not always what shaped them. To understand them more fully, we must move beyond inherited binaries and recover the larger civilizational landscape from which they emerged. Seen in that light, Kashmir’s history appears not merely as a contest for power but as a continuing search for identity, belonging, and modernity. Kashmir is more than a disputed territory. It is a civilization with an unusually long cultural memory. Over centuries, its distinctive ethos was formed through the interaction of diverse traditions, with Kashmir Shaivism providing one of its deepest philosophical foundations. More than a religious doctrine, it offers an ethical vision that celebrates human potential, the pursuit of knowledge, self-realization, and the unity of existence. It locates human excellence not in birth, creed, or gender, but in the cultivation of the mind and spirit. This inheritance formed an important part of the intellectual atmosphere in which Iqbal, Nehru, and Abdullah came of age. Their political paths diverged, sometimes sharply, but all three shared a profound faith in human agency and in the possibility of transforming society. Their influence rested not merely on political authority but on their ability to give voice to the aspirations of their people. To interpret them only through the categories of nationalism, communalism, or state power is to overlook the deeper cultural grammar that linked them. Their lives belong within the longue durée of Kashmir’s civilizational experience, where politics has always been intertwined with memory, culture, and moral imagination. One of the most remarkable features of modern Kashmir’s history is that Nehru, Abdullah, and Iqbal all sprang from the same broad civilizational roots in Kashmiri Pandit society. Nehru traced his ancestry to Raj Kaul. Abdullah’s lineage is linked to Raghav Kaul, whose descendants embraced Islam and became known as Sheikhs. Iqbal traced his ancestry to Sahaj Ram Sapru, whose family also converted to Islam. Their faiths diverged, but they remained heirs to the same intellectual tradition—one shaped by centuries of learning, philosophical reflection, and public debate. That shared inheritance profoundly influenced how each approached the question of Kashmir. What may seem surprising today becomes far less so when viewed beyond the layers of later political narratives and competing commentaries that have obscured this deeper continuity. History seldom advances through complete ruptures. It moves through continuity as much as change, carrying old inheritances into new identities. The lives of Nehru, Iqbal, and Abdullah illustrate this enduring truth. They differed profoundly over politics and the future of the subcontinent, yet all three inherited a cultural tradition that valued learning, argument, and public engagement. Iqbal, despite his political disagreements with Nehru, admired him as a serious intellectual whose engagement with India’s civilizational heritage reflected genuine philosophical depth. By contrast, he regarded Muhammad Ali Jinnah primarily as a constitutional lawyer and political strategist rather than a thinker concerned with the larger questions of history and civilization. Iqbal himself took quiet pride in his Kashmiri ancestry, seeing his Pandit lineage not as a contradiction of his Muslim identity but as an enduring source of intellectual inheritance. It is in this context that Iqbal’s reported advice to Sheikh Abdullah assumes a deeper significance. He is said to have urged Abdullah to maintain close relations with Nehru and to preserve his ties with the Kashmiri Pandit community. Whether this advice proved politically wise or historically prophetic may be debated. What matters more is the principle behind it: Iqbal understood that civilizational bonds often survive religious conversion and political conflict. Beneath changing identities lie older continuities that continue to shape societies long after political circumstances have changed. Their responses to modernity reveal this shared inheritance in different ways. Nehru envisioned a modern India founded upon scientific temper, secular democracy, and rational inquiry. Abdullah sought to harmonize democratic politics with the ethical and cultural traditions of Kashmiri society. Iqbal approached modernity as a philosophical challenge, welcoming its creative energies while insisting that it required moral and spiritual renewal. Their answers differed, but they were responding to the same historical question: how could inherited traditions engage a rapidly changing world without losing their moral centre? Read together, Nehru, Iqbal, and Abdullah represent a shared civilizational inheritance that transcended their different religious identities and political commitments. Though they belonged to different generations and confronted different historical circumstances, they drew from a common cultural repertoire that prized learning, dialogue, ethical reflection, and human creativity. Yet as nation-building gathered momentum, their lives and ideas were gradually absorbed into competing narratives of religion, nationalism, and state power. They came to be remembered less as participants in a shared intellectual tradition than as representatives of rival political visions. Perhaps this was inevitable. The twentieth century, shaped by nationalism, decolonization, and the ideological divisions of the Cold War, encouraged history to be read through rigid binaries. Biography yielded to ideology, and the subtle relationships that connected individuals were overshadowed by the dramatic struggles of state formation. Our own age offers a different vantage point. Globalization has compressed time and space, civilizational perspectives have re-entered scholarly debate, and inherited historical narratives are increasingly being revisited with fresh eyes. This changing intellectual climate invites us to read both history and biography differently. Seen from this perspective, the conversations, affinities, and disagreements among Nehru, Iqbal, and Abdullah assume a new significance. They remind us that history is not only the story of political conflict. It is also the story of ideas, memories, friendships, and shared cultural inheritances. Recovering these deeper continuities does not diminish the real differences among them. Rather, it allows us to understand those differences with greater depth and humanity. It also enables us to see Kashmir itself not simply as a political question, but as a civilization whose historical journey has been shaped by continuity as much as conflict. Viewed in this light, the intellectual journeys of Nehru, Iqbal, and Abdullah bear a striking resemblance to the philosophical imagination of Kashmir Shaivism. At its heart lies a refusal to see reality as fixed or complete. Existence is understood as a continuous process of becoming, where apparent opposites coexist in creative tension rather than being resolved into final certainties. Modernity, too, remains an unfinished project; always inviting criticism, renewal, and reinterpretation. In their different ways, all three men participated in this larger human endeavour, striving to reconcile inheritance with change and tradition with the demands of a new age. Their disagreements were real, but so too was the deeper civilizational world that they continued to share. Prof. Ashok Kaul, Retired Emeritus professor of Sociology at Banaras Hindu University.
